ECE 6390

Symbol errors and bit errors

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows why deciding on the right-hand or diagonal neighbor of the same transmitted point gives a different bit-error count.

An M-point alphabet carries m = log₂M coded bits per symbol. A symbol error occurs whenever the receiver selects the wrong point. Its bit cost depends on the transmitted and selected labels. Gray labeling makes neighboring labels differ by one bit, helping when nearest-neighbor errors dominate. In Fig. 1, read the horizontal I pair first and the vertical Q pair second. Dashed lines are decision boundaries halfway between adjacent coordinates.

For coherent square M-QAM, equally likely symbols, perfect timing and additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), put q = Q(√(3 Es/((M−1)N₀))) and a = 1−1/√M. The in-phase and quadrature coordinates are independent. Each coordinate is correct with probability 1−2 aq, so exact SER is Ps = 1−(1−2 aq)² = 4 aq−4 a²q².

At sufficiently high SNR with Gray labels, Pb ≈ 4 aq/log₂M. This approximation omits the squared-tail term and assumes mainly one wrong bit per nearest-neighbor error. The lecture’s compact 4 aQ expression is a nearest-neighbor SER approximation; treating it as an exact BER would confuse the two event counts.

For Gray QPSK, Es = 2 Eb and Pb = Q(√(Es/N₀)) = Q(√(2 Eb/N₀)), the same ideal BER as BPSK at equal energy per bit. Equal energy per symbol instead gives QPSK half as much energy per bit. The plotted QAM formula applies to square grids; APSK rings require their own detection model.

Example

For square 16-QAM at Es/N₀ = 10 (10 dB), q = Q(√2) ≈ 0.07865 and a =0.75. Exact SER is about 0.2220, while the high-SNR Gray-BER approximation is about 0.05899. At this modest SNR, the approximation assumptions deserve attention.

Practice

1. Can a measured 10% symbol-error fraction alone determine the bit-error fraction of 16-QAM?

Count bits changed by each incorrect decision.

Additional labeling and error-transition information is needed. Each wrong symbol can change different numbers of its four bits.

2. Why do BPSK and Gray QPSK agree on an Eb/N₀ plot but differ on an Es/N₀ plot?

QPSK divides a symbol’s energy between two orthogonal bit coordinates.

Uncoded QPSK has two bits per symbol, so Es =2 Eb. Equal bit energy yields the same coordinate detection problem; equal symbol energy gives each QPSK bit half as much energy.
